strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: PTQ for DiT-based Real-ISR, claimed as the first systematic PTQ exploration for this task, with a clear articulation of the three challenges (detail loss from low-rank approximation, calibration-heavy mixed precision, static activation precision across timesteps).

Well-motivated technical design: H-SVD combines a global low-rank branch with block-wise rank-1 local branches under a matched parameter budget; VaSMP derives a closed-form, data-free bit allocation from a rate-distortion argument (Eqs. 12-16); VaTMP solves a piecewise-constant timestep scheduling problem via dynamic programming under an average-bit budget (Eqs. 18-23). The components are each grounded in explicit distortion modeling.

Extensive empirical comparison: results on four standard Real-ISR benchmarks (DrealSR, RealSR, RealLR200, RealLQ250) under both W4A6 and W4A4, against many recent baselines (SVDQuant, QuaRot, FlatQuant, Q-DiT, PTQ4DiT, QueST, PassionSR, EfficientDM, Q-Diffusion).

Per-component ablations (Tables 2-4) are present and show each part contributes; the PCA analysis in Fig. 4 and the variance distribution analysis in Figs. 5-6 provide empirical motivation for the design choices. Calibration overhead is genuinely small (32 LR-only crops).
The paper honestly notes limitations of NR-IQA metrics under heavy quantization and disables VaTMP when unnecessary (W4A6), suggesting careful experimental practice.
weaknesses: Efficiency comparison is potentially misleading: Q-DiT4SR keeps FP low-rank branches (465M params / 2,776G ops vs. 359M / 2,664G for QuaRot and QueST in Fig. 1). The headline 5.8x size and 6.14x ops reductions are relative to FP, but relative to competing quantization methods the model is larger and does more compute, and the FP branches cannot benefit from INT kernels. No wall-clock latency or memory measurements are reported; only theoretical FLOPs/params. This should be reported and discussed for the efficiency claims to be fully supported.

SOTA claim is overstated for W4A4: Table 1(b) shows Q-DiT4SR loses to SVDQuant on LPIPS for RealSR (0.3665 vs 0.3268) and to FP on several MANIQA entries (e.g., Q-Diffusion 0.4991 vs FP 0.4483 vs Q-DiT4SR 0.4030 on DrealSR), and the W4A6 MANIQA/ClipIQA on some datasets also favor FP. The paper partially acknowledges metric unreliability, but 'SOTA under both settings' is not uniformly supported per metric; a more nuanced claim (e.g., best average or best perceptual consistency) would be more accurate.

Validation is limited to a single backbone (DiT4SR) at a single scale (x4); generalization to other DiT-based SR models (e.g., DreamClear) or settings is not demonstrated, weakening the framing as a general framework for DiT-based Real-ISR.

The theoretical machinery rests on per-token Gaussianity after Hadamard rotation and per-channel Gaussianity of weights; the quality of these approximations is asserted (Eq. 1) but not empirically validated, and the rate-distortion analysis ignores the effect of weight distortion on output/end-task error, which the authors' own MP-baseline ablation suggests matters.
Inconsistent configurations across settings (VaTMP on for W4A4 but off for W4A6; softmax fixed at 8-bit) complicate attribution and comparability with baselines that use uniform precision.

Presentation gaps: the abstract ends with an incomplete code URL; Figure 1 reports params/ops only for four of the compared methods; the calibration set is drawn from the RealSR training split while overlap policies with test data are not explicitly discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant problem: post-training quantization of DiT-based Real-ISR models, which sit between U-Net SR diffusion models (existing SR quantization) and text-to-image DiTs (existing DiT quantization).

The method is well organized around three complementary components (H-SVD weight decomposition, VaSMP data-free weight mixed precision, VaTMP DP-based temporal activation precision), each with a stated motivation (rate-distortion reasoning, variance statistics) and a dedicated ablation (Tables 2-4, Figs. 5-6, 8-9).

The evaluation is broad: four standard Real-ISR benchmarks (DrealSR, RealSR, RealLR200, RealLQ250), ten competing PTQ/PEFT methods across W4A6 and W4A4 settings, plus qualitative comparisons and an honest observation about IQA metric unreliability for quantized diffusion SR.
VaSMP's calibration-free weight bit allocation and VaTMP's tiny 32-image LR-only calibration are attractive for deployment compared to reconstruction-heavy baselines.
weaknesses: The headline efficiency claims are undermined by the method's own accounting. Fig. 1 reports Q-DiT4SR at 465M params / 2,776G ops versus SVDQuant at 359M / 2,664G — i.e., the proposed method is larger and more expensive than its closest competitor, and its parameter count is essentially the same as the FP model (465M), because the FP SVD-G and SVD-L branches offset quantization savings. The claimed '5.8x size reduction' is never reconciled with these numbers; how much memory the FP branches consume is not analyzed.

The 'SOTA performance' claim is not supported by the tables. Under W4A4, SVDQuant achieves better LPIPS on 3 of 4 datasets (e.g., 0.3268 vs 0.3665 on RealSR; 0.3821 vs 0.4327 on DrealSR), and EfficientDM substantially beats Q-DiT4SR on MANIQA on nearly all settings (e.g., 0.5027 vs 0.4378 in W4A6; 0.5154 vs 0.4265 in W4A4 on RealLR200). The results are mixed across metrics; calling this SOTA requires more careful argument than the paper provides, especially while simultaneously arguing IQA metrics can be misleading.

Only a single backbone (DiT4SR) is evaluated. Given the paper's framing as the first PTQ framework for DiT-based Real-ISR, generality across at least one other DiT SR architecture (e.g., DreamClear) is needed to support the framework claim; as it stands this is an exploration on one model.

No actual deployment measurements are reported. For an efficiency/deployment-motivated paper, there is no wall-clock latency, kernel-level speedup, or peak-memory result — only FLOPs/params. Moreover, VaTMP's per-(layer, timestep) activation bit-width schedule (Fig. 9) implies dynamic-precision execution that is non-trivial to realize on current hardware; its practical cost is not discussed.

The variance-based sensitivity proxies are validated only indirectly. VaSMP's distortion model (Eq. 13) is a weight-only proxy with no end-to-end evidence that mean output-channel variance predicts downstream SR quality, and Fig. 5 is a qualitative boxplot rather than a correlation analysis. The connection between quantization distortion and perceptual SR quality is assumed, not established.

Several methodological details are underspecified, weakening reproducibility: baseline numbers are not stated to be re-run on the DiT4SR backbone (consistent-comparison protocol unclear); the greedy discretization of VaSMP and block-size search space for SVD-L lack exact procedures; the clip constant alpha in Eq. 12 and the kappa(b) computation are not fully specified; no random seeds/variance are reported for the stochastic SR pipeline; code is promised but not available at review time.

The ablation in Table 2 shows the SVD-L budget trades parameters directly for quality (454.78M to 529.06M from rank 4 to 32), which means H-SVD buys quality with extra FP parameters rather than under a strictly fixed budget as the matched-budget narrative in Sec. 3.2 suggests.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and timely problem: aggressive low-bit PTQ for DiT-based Real-ISR, for which no dedicated framework existed. The three components (H-SVD, VaSMP, VaTMP) are coherently motivated and mapped one-to-one onto the three stated challenges.

The methodology is technically sound and clearly presented. The variance-based bit allocation (VaSMP) has a clean rate-distortion derivation (Eqs. 12-16) leading to a closed-form continuous solution plus a practical greedy discretization, and VaTMP's piecewise-constant timestep scheduling via dynamic programming (Eqs. 18-23) is a sensible formulation of the temporal mixed-precision problem.

Evaluation breadth is good: four standard real-world SR benchmarks, two aggressive settings (W4A6, W4A4), ten baselines spanning general PTQ, DiT-specific PTQ, SR-specific PTQ, and PEFT methods, plus ablations of each component (Tables 2-4) and a rank-budget trade-off analysis.

The paper is largely honest about weaknesses in the evaluation protocol: it explicitly notes that no-reference IQA metrics can reward visibly noisy reconstructions (Sec. 4.2), and it is transparent that calibration data is required only for VaTMP (32 LR crops) while VaSMP is data-free.

Good empirical practice: the motivation experiments (PCA analysis in Fig. 4, variance distributions in Figs. 5-6) provide concrete evidence that inter-layer weight variance heterogeneity and timestep-dependent activation variance actually exist in this backbone, supporting the design of the mixed-precision schemes.
weaknesses: The central 'SOTA' claim is weakened by the full-reference results. On LPIPS — the only full-reference perceptual metric used — Q-DiT4SR is slightly worse than SVDQuant under both W4A6 (0.3386 vs 0.3371 on RealSR) and W4A4 (0.3665 vs 0.3268 on RealSR, a non-trivial gap). Since the paper itself argues that no-reference IQA metrics (MUSIQ/MANIQA/CLIPIQA/LIQE) can be unreliable for heavily quantized diffusion models, most of the headline superiority in Table 1 rests on metrics the authors distrust. The claim that Q-DiT4SR 'achieves SOTA performance' is therefore not fully supported by the most trustworthy metric.

The reported efficiency gains (5.8x size, 6.14x ops) are for compression relative to FP, but Q-DiT4SR actually uses more parameters (465M) and operations (2,776G) than SVDQuant (359M/2,664G) at the same nominal bit-width, because of the FP low-rank branches. The paper never reports wall-clock latency or memory measurements; per-timestep, per-layer variable bit-widths (VaTMP) may not translate into real speedups without specialized kernels, and this deployment-relevant question is left unaddressed for a paper motivated by 'real-world deployment'.

Generality is untested: all experiments use a single backbone (DiT4SR). Given that DreamClear and other DiT-SR models exist, and given that VaSMP's data-free bit allocation depends on backbone-specific variance statistics (Fig. 5), it is unclear whether the findings transfer. Similarly, VaTMP's premise that 'cross-layer activation mixed precision is unreliable' is asserted rather than demonstrated with an ablation of cross-layer (spatial) activation precision.

The Gaussian-per-token assumption after Hadamard transform (Eq. 1) and the resulting distortion models are approximations whose validity for SR activations (which drive texture fidelity) is shown only qualitatively via KDE in one layer (Fig. 6). No analysis of when the variance-based sensitivity proxy fails (e.g., layers where variance is low but quantization error is perceptually amplified) is provided.

Several experimental details are under-specified: the bit candidate set for VaSMP weights (b_min/b_max), how the H-SVD block-size search resolves the inequality in Eq. (9), and how the FP low-rank branches are kept out of the quantized compute path. Reproducibility currently rests on a code promise, which is not yet verifiable.
Limitations are not explicitly discussed in a dedicated section; the metric-reliability caveat and single-backbone scope should be surfaced there rather than buried in the results narrative.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and previously unexplored problem: PTQ for DiT-based Real-ISR, where existing quantization methods (designed for U-Net diffusion or text-to-image DiTs) degrade severely. The claim of being the first systematic PTQ framework for DiT-based Real-ISR appears plausible given the related work survey.

Technical design is coherent and well-motivated: H-SVD decomposes weights into a global low-rank branch plus a block-wise rank-1 local branch under a matched parameter budget; VaSMP derives a closed-form, data-free weight bit allocation from the standard high-rate quantization distortion model (Eq. 12-16); VaTMP schedules activation precision across timesteps via dynamic programming under an average-bit budget (Eq. 18-23). Each component targets one of the three clearly articulated failure modes.

Comprehensive evaluation: four real-world benchmarks (DrealSR, RealSR, RealLR200, RealLQ250), two aggressive settings (W4A6, W4A4), ten baselines including recent DiT-specific (PTQ4DiT, Q-DiT, SVDQuant, FlatQuant, QueST) and SR-specific (PassionSR) methods, plus ablations for each component (Tables 2-4), runtime/memory profiling (Tables 5-6), backbone generalization to DreamClear (Table 7), calibration-set robustness (Table 8), and an ROI-level artifact analysis (Table 9).

Exceptionally honest limitations discussion (Sec. 4.6): admits residual artifacts on thin/repetitive/high-contrast textures under W4A4, admits the implementation does not use native arbitrary-precision kernels, and cautions that IQA metric gains over FP may reflect metric unreliability rather than genuine improvement. The calibration robustness experiment (Table 8) is a nice touch supporting the claim that VaTMP relies on generic variance patterns.

Practical system contributions are reported concretely: measured 4.51x end-to-end speedup, memory reduction from ~15GB to ~4GB, with a runtime breakdown attributing the gap from the theoretical 6.14x to non-quantized ops, and implementation details (Triton kernel for SVD-L, branch-parallel SVD-G).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The backbone machinery (Hadamard transform, FP low-rank branch + quantized residual, per-output-channel scaling) is directly inherited from SVDQuant/RobuQ/QuaRot; H-SVD is essentially a block-wise rank-1 augmentation of the existing low-rank branch under a matched budget. The VaSMP closed-form bit allocation (Eq. 14-16) is a textbook rate-distortion water-filling result applied with variance statistics, and VaTMP applies the same distortion model temporally via standard DP. The contribution is a sensible combination and adaptation to a new domain rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The distortion model underlying VaSMP is weight-space Frobenius distortion and is not output- or task-sensitive: it ignores the interaction between weight and activation quantization errors and the actual activation covariance per layer. The paper's own ablation (Table 3) shows H-SVD alone (67.46 MUSIQ) outperforms H-SVD + MP, and VaSMP's gains over a well-tuned output-sensitive allocation are not clearly isolated against stronger sensitivity criteria (e.g., Hessian traces or activation-weighted objectives).

The deployment story for mixed precision is under-specified and partially undermines the efficiency claims: the authors concede that VaSMP/VaTMP bit-widths are 'mapped to standard low-bit linear computations' rather than native arbitrary-precision kernels. It is unclear how 3/5-bit weight layers or per-timestep 3/4/5-bit activation schedules actually execute and yield speedup at inference; measured end-to-end speedup (4.5x) and memory are actually slightly worse than SVDQuant (4.8x, 3723 MiB vs 3975 MiB), so the practical advantage rests entirely on reconstruction quality.

Quality gains under the headline W4A4 setting are modest and metric-inconsistent: LPIPS degrades from 0.3179 (FP) to 0.3665, and on several metrics baselines score comparably or better (e.g., MANIQA values >0.5 for Q-Diffusion/EfficientDM/PTQ4DiT vs 0.4367 for Q-DiT4SR), which the authors attribute to NR-IQA unreliability but this is not resolved. Some W4A6 results even exceed FP (e.g., MUSIQ 70.36 vs 70.33; DreamClear W4A6 LPIPS/MUSIQ better than FP), which the paper interprets only speculatively as a 'perceptual regularizer'.

Baseline fairness concerns: several baselines were designed for other architectures or regimes (Q-Diffusion for U-Net diffusion, PassionSR for one-step SR models, FlatQuant for LLMs), and the paper does not state whether baselines were re-tuned for DiT4SR or evaluated with default settings. The multi-step/timestep count of DiT4SR inference and sampler details are not reported, which affects reproducibility of the temporal scheduling.

Reproducibility gaps despite a code promise: the abstract's code URL is empty; key hyperparameters such as the block size search result (the chosen (so, si)), bit-width ranges (bmin/bmax) for VaSMP, DP segment granularity, and calibration specifics beyond '32 images, 128x128 crops' are not fully specified. The impact statement is boilerplate, though no serious ethical concerns arise for this application domain.

The theory is approximate in ways not quantified: the Gaussian assumption after Hadamard transform (Eq. 1), high-rate approximation (Eq. 12), and independent per-output-channel error treatment (Eq. 13) are heuristics for real DiT activations with outliers; no empirical validation of the predicted vs. actual distortion is provided beyond variance distribution figures.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: post-training quantization for DiT-based Real-ISR, and the claim of being the first systematic PTQ framework for this setting appears plausible given the related-work coverage.

The method decomposition is sensible and clearly presented: H-SVD (global low-rank + block-wise rank-1 local branch under a matched parameter budget), VaSMP (data-free, variance-driven cross-layer weight bit allocation derived from standard high-rate quantization distortion analysis), and VaTMP (DP-based temporal activation bit scheduling), each mapped to one of the three identified challenges.

Comprehensive empirical protocol: four real-world benchmarks, comparisons against ten recent PTQ/PEFT baselines under W4A6 and W4A4, ablations for each component, calibration-set robustness checks (Table 8), generalization to a second backbone (DreamClear, Table 7), and an ROI-level artifact analysis (Table 9).

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper acknowledges residual W4A4 artifacts, the mismatch between no-reference IQA metrics and perceptual quality in heavily quantized diffusion SR, the caution needed when interpreting W4A6 > FP scores, and the fact that mixed-precision schedules are currently mapped to standard kernels rather than native arbitrary-precision kernels.

Practical profiling (Tables 5-6) is informative, including the honest note that the 6.14× theoretical operation reduction translates to 4.51× end-to-end speedup due to unquantized components, and that the H-SVD branch costs ~3% latency and slightly more memory than SVDQuant.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: each component is a relatively direct combination of established techniques — Hadamard rotation and low-rank+residual decomposition follow SVDQuant/QuaRot/RobuQ, temporal bit scheduling follows TDQ, and the variance-based allocation is a closed-form consequence of the standard E[e²] ∝ σ²·2^(-2b) approximation. The main contribution is adaptation to a new task rather than a new mechanism, and the theoretical derivations (Eqs. 12-22) are straightforward applications of known results.

Evaluation reliability is weakened by the authors' own admission: several baselines achieve visibly noisy reconstructions yet score competitively or better on MANIQA (e.g., under W4A4 on DrealSR, Q-Diffusion 0.4991 and EfficientDM 0.4921 vs. 0.4030 for Q-DiT4SR), and the paper concedes a metric-perception mismatch. This substantially undermines unqualified 'SOTA under W4A4' claims; the W4A4 results are mixed rather than dominant (LPIPS degrades from 0.3897 to 0.4327 on DrealSR, and MUSIQ/LIQE are below FP).

The main experiments use a single backbone (DiT4SR); DreamClear (Table 7) is a welcome but thinner generalization check with some metrics below FP even at W4A6 (MUSIQ 62.94 vs 57.77, LIQE 3.472 vs 3.082), which the authors explain via a speculative 'perceptual regularizer' argument rather than direct evidence.

The Gaussianity assumption underlying both the weight quantizer design (Eq. 1-3) and the VaTMP clipping/distortion model (Eqs. 18-20) is asserted and empirically motivated only loosely (KDE plots); no quantitative validation of the distortion model's predictive accuracy against measured quantization error is provided.

Motivating evidence for H-SVD is largely indirect (PCA removal experiments in Fig. 4, output-space projections); there is no analysis of when the block-wise rank-1 branch helps versus hurts, and the rank-budget ablation shows diminishing/negative returns beyond rank 8, suggesting the design space is tuned empirically rather than understood.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code-release URL is a dangling placeholder ('will be available at'), and key implementation details (block-size search outcomes for SVD-L, exact DP formulation for VaTMP segments, calibration statistics collection procedure under the quantized pipeline) are underspecified.

Some claims are imprecise: the abstract emphasizes 5.8×/6.14× reductions that largely follow from the backbone choice plus mixed precision rather than the proposed components, and Fig. 1 reports identical Params/Ops for SVDQuant and Q-DiT4SR while the text claims advantages from H-SVD's budget-matching, which is confusing without explicit accounting.

strengths: Addresses a relevant, under-explored problem: post-training quantization for DiT-based Real-ISR, which existing DiT quantization methods (designed for text-to-image) and U-Net SR quantization methods do not directly cover. The claim of being the first systematic PTQ framework for this setting appears plausible given the related work coverage.

The proposed H-SVD is clearly motivated: the paper provides an empirical PCA analysis (Fig. 4) showing that removing dominant principal components degrades SR quality and that the hierarchical decomposition better aligns with the FP output space under a matched parameter budget, giving the design a principled rationale rather than pure heuristics.

VaSMP derives a closed-form, data-free bit allocation from rate-distortion theory (Eqs. 12-16), and the variance distribution analysis (Fig. 5) empirically supports the key assumption that Hadamard-transformed weight variances vary strongly across layers but stay stable within a layer. This is a clean, computationally cheap alternative to Hessian- or reconstruction-based mixed precision.

Comprehensive evaluation: four real-world benchmarks, two bit settings (W4A6 and W4A4), ten baselines, ablations of each component (Tables 2-4), backbone generalization to DreamClear (Table 7), calibration-set robustness across domains (Table 8), and an ROI-level artifact analysis (Table 9). Q-DiT4SR is consistently at or near the top across metrics and settings.

Practical profiling is a strength: the paper reports real peak memory (Table 5), a runtime breakdown attributing the gap between the theoretical 6.14x and measured 4.51x speedup to unquantized ops (Table 6), and explains the engineering behind the Triton/Monarch-style SVD-L kernel. This goes beyond what many PTQ papers provide.

Honest limitations discussion: the paper acknowledges remaining W4A4 artifacts on thin/repetitive textures, the absence of native arbitrary-precision kernels, and metric reliability issues in no-reference IQA (Sec. 4.2), and interprets the W4A6 gains over FP on DreamClear cautiously rather than overclaiming.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty relative to prior work. The quantization backbone (Hadamard rotation + FP low-rank branch + quantized residual with per-channel scaling) is essentially SVDQuant (Li et al., 2024); VaTMP's timestep-wise bit allocation is conceptually close to Temporal Dynamic Quantization (So et al., 2023); and VaSMP's allocation is a classical closed-form rate-distortion bit assignment. The genuinely new elements are the block-wise rank-1 local branch under a matched budget and the variance-based, calibration-free scheduling criteria, which are well-executed but incremental.

Efficiency comparison with the closest baseline is unfavorable on some axes: Figure 1 reports Q-DiT4SR at 465M params / 2,776G ops versus SVDQuant at 359M / 2,664G, and Table 5 shows Q-DiT4SR uses more memory (3974.64 vs 3722.83 MiB) with slightly lower speedup (~4.5x vs ~4.8x). The advantage over SVDQuant therefore rests entirely on reconstruction quality; the paper should discuss this trade-off more explicitly.

Several derivations rest on assumptions that are asserted rather than validated: the per-token Gaussianity after Hadamard transform ('under some assumptions', Eq. 1), the high-rate quantization approximation (Eq. 12), and the restriction of VaTMP schedules to piecewise-constant segments. No experiment quantifies how far these assumptions hold for Real-ISR activations, so the theoretical motivation for VaSMP/VaTMP is more suggestive than rigorous.

Metric reliability undermines some conclusions. In Table 1(b), several visibly degraded baselines (Q-Diffusion, EfficientDM, PTQ4DiT) obtain MANIQA scores above the FP model (~0.50-0.52 vs 0.462), and the paper itself notes a perceptual-metric mismatch. Since SOTA claims lean on these no-reference IQA metrics, and Table 4 even shows VaSMP degrading LIQE relative to baseline (3.091 vs 3.191), the evaluation would benefit from a human study or distortion-based metrics (e.g., ROI-PSNR extended to more conditions) to substantiate the perceptual claims.

Some implementation details are underspecified for reproducibility: the exact search over block sizes S (Eq. 8) and its complexity, the greedy discretization tie-breaking, the DP formulation for VaTMP beyond the segment cost definition, and details of the spatio-temporal grid deployment are not fully described. Code is promised ('will be available at' with no link), so reproducibility currently depends on the authors' follow-through.

The 'first PTQ framework for DiT-based Real-ISR' claim is hard to verify and sits in tension with PassionSR (Zhu et al., 2025), which the paper positions as a one-step SR-specific PTQ method; the distinction rests on the DiT backbone and multi-step setting, which should be stated more precisely.

Generalization results are thinner than the main results: Table 7 evaluates only DreamClear on RealSR (single dataset, no comparison against baselines under the same conditions), so the claim that the framework is backbone-agnostic is supported but only lightly.
